frozen_original.title: Sloman Documents Political Pressure from Trump on Epstein's 2008 Non-Prosecution Agreement
frozen_original.synopsis: Jeffrey H. Sloman, former second-in-command to U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta, stated in documents released by House Oversight that the 2008 Epstein non-prosecution agreement was structured in secret, and specifically references Donald Trump and other senior officials among those who exerted pressure to secure the lenient deal. The NPA limited Epstein to 13 months in county jail — allowing him work release 6 days a week — and granted immunity from federal prosecution to 'any potential co-conspirators,' a clause that has never been fully explained. The Sloman documents represent the most direct allegation that Trump personally influenced the deal that kept Epstein out of federal prison for a decade.

primary.title: DOJ Found Poor Judgment in Acosta's Epstein Non-Prosecution Agreement
primary.description_short: The Epstein agreement was signed on September 24, 2007; DOJ later found Acosta used poor judgment, but no improper factors or professional misconduct.
primary.description_medium: Jeffrey Epstein's federal non-prosecution agreement was signed on September 24, 2007, as a state-based resolution of the federal investigation. DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility later found that Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in choosing that resolution and in failing to ensure victims received notice, but said the decision fell within his discretion and was not based on improper factors. The reviewed report excerpt does not corroborate the original card's separate allegation of direct Trump pressure.
primary.description_long: DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility documents that the federal investigation into Jeffrey Epstein was resolved through a non-prosecution agreement signed on September 24, 2007. The agreement ended the Southern District of Florida's federal investigation and forwent federal prosecution of Epstein, four named co-conspirators, and “any potential co-conspirators”; victims were not informed or consulted before signing. In 2020, OPR concluded that then-U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in resolving the case through the agreement and in failing to ensure that Florida would notify victims about the state plea hearing. OPR also said Acosta acted within his broad discretion, found no improper factors behind the decision, and did not find professional misconduct. This card keeps the documented agreement and review outcome while removing the unsupported assertion that Jeffrey Sloman documented direct political pressure from Donald Trump. The accessed DOJ report excerpt does not independently establish that Trump intervened, nor does it establish the opposite; that question remains outside this supported copy. The date follows the agreement's signing, not Epstein's June 2008 state-court plea.

frozen_original.title: Trump Uses 'Bigly' Unironically at Presidential Debate
frozen_original.synopsis: During the 2016 presidential debates, Trump used the non-standard word 'bigly' — or a phrase that sounded like it — in what appeared to be an unironic expression, prompting widespread mockery and debate about whether he said 'big league' or actually said 'bigly.' The word 'bigly' technically exists as an archaic adverb but has been out of common use for centuries. Regardless of what Trump intended, the episode became a viral internet phenomenon and emblematic of his idiosyncratic relationship with the English language. Linguistic analysts noted that Trump's vocabulary and sentence structure in the debates was notably limited compared to other presidential candidates. The 'bigly' moment became shorthand for critiques of Trump's verbal facility.

primary.title: At the 2016 Debate, Trump Said He Would Cut Taxes “Big League”
primary.description_short: The official transcript records Trump saying “big league,” not “bigly,” while discussing taxes and regulation at the September 2016 debate.
primary.description_medium: At the September 26, 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, Trump argued about taxes and regulation. The Commission on Presidential Debates transcript records him saying, “I’m going to cut taxes big league,” and then saying Clinton would “raise taxes big league.” It does not record the word “bigly,” so this entry should use “big league” and avoid claims about audience reaction or Trump’s language ability that the transcript does not establish.
primary.description_long: During the first 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, moderator Lester Holt moved the candidates through a discussion of prosperity and economic plans. In that exchange, Donald Trump criticized Hillary Clinton’s tax and regulatory proposals, then said: “I’m going to cut regulations. I’m going to cut taxes big league, and you’re going to raise taxes big league, end of story.” The Commission on Presidential Debates transcript therefore supports “big league” as the phrase used in this sentence. It does not support a claim that Trump said “bigly” here. This correction is narrow: it records the wording in the official transcript and does not decide what Trump intended, whether listeners misheard it, or how widely a later interpretation circulated. The packet offers no verified evidence for the old card’s claims that this phrase became a viral phenomenon or a measure of Trump’s vocabulary. Treat this as an accurately quoted debate remark, not as evidence of a policy, legal violation, or lasting public effect.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends Free School Lunch Program Expansion
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration reversed Biden-era expansions of the National School Lunch Program that had extended free meals to millions of additional low-income children. The rollback included eliminating community eligibility provisions that had allowed high-poverty schools to serve all students free meals regardless of individual applications, as well as reversing summer food service program expansions. An estimated 4 to 5 million children who had been receiving free school meals under the expanded program lost that benefit. Child hunger organizations documented immediate increases in children coming to school without having eaten. Nutritionists and pediatricians warned the cuts would exacerbate food insecurity, harm cognitive development, and increase school absenteeism among children in low-income families.

primary.title: House Republicans Proposed Tightening Universal School-Meal Eligibility
primary.description_short: A March 2025 House Republican budget proposal would raise the school-meal CEP threshold from 25% to 60%.
primary.description_medium: Chalkbeat reported that a House Republican budget proposal would raise the Community Eligibility Provision threshold from 25% to 60%. An advocacy-group estimate cited in the report projected that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected. The story describes a proposal, not an enacted March rollback.
primary.description_long: On March 12, 2025, Chalkbeat reported that House Republicans were considering a budget proposal to make schools meet a stricter threshold before using the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), which lets qualifying schools serve meals at no charge to all enrolled students. At the time, the minimum identified-student percentage was 25 percent under USDA’s 2023 final rule. The proposal described in the report would raise the threshold to 60 percent. Chalkbeat attributed to an advocacy organization the estimate that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected. Those figures were projected consequences of a proposal, not measured losses after an enacted rule. The sources reviewed do not establish that USDA completed a March 2025 cancellation of CEP, that 4 to 5 million children immediately lost meals, or that families experienced the harms stated in the frozen synopsis. This repaired entry therefore describes the threatened eligibility change and identifies Congress as the source of the proposal; it does not attribute a completed rollback to the Trump administration or state that the proposal itself became law.

source_fact_map.quote: The House Republican proposal would raise the share to 60% — higher than the threshold has ever been. That would kick more than 24,000 schools off of community eligibility, and some 12 million students would no longer automatically qualify for free meals, Hysom’s organization estimated.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: One proposal would dramatically increase the share of students who need to be enrolled in aid programs — such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families — for schools to be eligible to serve free meals to all kids through the Community Eligibility Provision. Right now, schools need to show 25% of students are enrolled in those kinds of assistance programs to participate in community eligibility. The House Republican proposal would raise the share to 60% — higher than the threshold has ever been. That would kick more than 24,000 schools off of community eligibility, and some 12 million students would no longer automatically qualify for free meals, Hysom’s organization estimated.

corrected_proposal.title: House Republicans Proposed Tightening Universal School-Meal Eligibility
corrected_proposal.description_short: A March 2025 House Republican budget proposal would raise the school-meal CEP threshold from 25% to 60%.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Chalkbeat reported that a House Republican budget proposal would raise the Community Eligibility Provision threshold from 25% to 60%. An advocacy-group estimate cited in the report projected that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected. The story describes a proposal, not an enacted March rollback.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 12, 2025, Chalkbeat reported that House Republicans were considering a budget proposal to raise the Community Eligibility Provision’s minimum identified-student percentage from 25 percent to 60 percent. The provision lets qualifying schools serve meals at no charge to all enrolled students. The 25 percent threshold came from USDA’s 2023 final rule. Chalkbeat cited an advocacy group’s estimate that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected if the threshold changed. Those figures described projected exposure under a proposal, not a count of students who lost meals. The report did not describe an enacted USDA rollback or an immediate removal of free meals. The proposal concerned a potential eligibility change; the available sources do not establish that it became law or that schools stopped serving meals because of it. Schools below the proposed threshold could lose eligibility if the change were enacted.
